Dojos are neutral settlements where the player and AI can recruit students, purchase martial manuals that improve combat skills, join a specific school, or duel instructors for rank and reputation. Each dojo follows a distinct martial lineage. Improving relations with a dojo strengthens relations with all dojos of that lineage, and may improve standing with their sponsoring domain.

Itto-ryu is a prestigious family of kenjutsu schools emphasizing the principle of the 'one sword.' Practitioners, known as Itto-ryu kenshi, focus on decisive cuts, proper distancing, and timing. During the late Bakumatsu, its instructors were sought after by domains and samurai for dueling, military training, and personal defense.

Hokushin Itto-ryu is the northern branch of Itto-ryu, combining classical swordsmanship with battlefield practicality. Practitioners train in katana, wakizashi, and naginata, honing timing, distance, and decisive strikes. In the late Bakumatsu, the school supplied instructors to northern domain militias and duelists in Edo.

Shinkage-ryu is a transformative kenjutsu lineage that emphasizes strategy, posture, and subtlety. Practitioners wield katana and wakizashi, focusing on psychological control and precision. In the Bakumatsu period, Shinkage-ryu influenced many derivative schools, including Taisha-ryu, and trained elite duelists and samurai instructors.

Jigen-ryu, originating in Satsuma, is known for ferocious, lightning-fast attacks with katana and odachi. Practitioners cultivate power, speed, and relentless offense. In the late Bakumatsu, Jigen-ryu kenshi were recognized for their role in domain defense and martial competitions, embodying the martial spirit of southern Japan.

Hozoin-ryu specializes in spearmanship, particularly the cross-shaped jumonji-yari and naginata. Practitioners train in precise thrusts, fluid footwork, and battlefield awareness. By the Bakumatsu era, instructors trained domain militias and dueling students, maintaining a reputation for technical elegance and deadly efficiency.

Tanegashima-ryu is a firearms school teaching the use of matchlock arquebuses. Practitioners learn coordinated volleys and battlefield deployment. In late Tokugawa Japan, Tanegashima-ryu instructors were vital in domain militias, bridging traditional martial culture and early modern warfare.

Takashima-ryu teaches modern firearms techniques, emphasizing disciplined firing methods and unit coordination. Practitioners prepared for the changing nature of war during the Bakumatsu period, integrating Western rifles into traditional martial education for domain forces.

Heki-ryu is a classical archery school, teaching yumi mastery for battlefield and ceremonial use. Practitioners develop accuracy, composure, and situational awareness. In the late Bakumatsu, Heki-ryu archers served both militarily and ceremonially, maintaining the prominence of mounted and foot archery traditions.

Shinto Munen-ryu is a kenjutsu school emphasizing adaptability, speed, and fluid techniques with katana and wakizashi. Practitioners were trained for dueling and skirmishes, preparing samurai and retainers for the unpredictable conflicts of the Bakumatsu era.

Ogasawara-ryu is the classical school of mounted archery and etiquette, teaching yumi mastery on horseback. Practitioners develop poise, precision, and ceremonial bearing, serving as both martial and noble instructors in the late Tokugawa period.

Hoki-ryu is a kenjutsu school specializing in katana techniques. Practitioners cultivate strong cutting, timing, and defensive skills. During the Bakumatsu, Hoki-ryu instructors trained samurai and domain forces, ensuring readiness in duels and military engagements.

Shingyoto-ryu teaches a combination of katana, odachi, and naginata, focusing on versatility and battlefield adaptability. Practitioners excel in both dueling and larger engagements, sustaining their relevance through the late Bakumatsu period.

Oshima-ryu is a multi-weapon school specializing in yari, naginata, and variations such as jumonji and kagi yari. Practitioners develop complex thrusting and footwork techniques, serving as capable battlefield instructors during the late Tokugawa period.

Tamiya-ryu focuses on the long-hilted nagae katana, training practitioners in precise strikes and extended reach. The school's methods were valued for dueling and defensive combat by samurai in the late Bakumatsu era.

Moriuchi-ryu is a mounted martial school emphasizing yari and katana techniques. Practitioners develop coordination, balance, and tactical awareness for cavalry operations. In the Bakumatsu period, Moriuchi-ryu trained domain cavalry and retainers in practical combat skills.

Owari Kan-ryu specializes in the sliding kuda-yari, offering innovative spear techniques. Practitioners train in precision, timing, and footwork. The school's unique weapons and methods were valued by Owari samurai for both ceremonial and battlefield purposes.

Shinshin-ryu is a kenjutsu school teaching katana and wakizashi techniques with an emphasis on timing and adaptability. Practitioners excel in duels and personal defense, maintaining a respected position among samurai in the late Bakumatsu.

Tatsumi-ryu is a comprehensive martial school training practitioners in katana, wakizashi, yari, naginata, and shuriken. The school's broad curriculum prepared samurai for dueling, battlefield, and self-defense during the Bakumatsu period.

Tennen Rishin-ryu is a kenjutsu school focusing on katana, wakizashi, and occasional yari use. Practitioners were famously associated with the Shinsengumi, combining practical swordsmanship with rigorous discipline in the late Bakumatsu era.

Nanbu-ryu is a mounted martial school emphasizing bow and sword techniques. Practitioners develop horseback combat skills, coordination, and precision. In the Bakumatsu period, Nanbu-ryu kenshi served as cavalry instructors and domain retainers.

Kyoshin Meiichi-ryu is a kenjutsu school emphasizing katana and wakizashi mastery. Practitioners cultivate precise cutting, timing, and fluid technique. In the Bakumatsu era, Kyoshin Meiichi-ryu trained loyalists and aspiring samurai in practical swordsmanship for both duels and domain service.

Change did not come to Japan all at once. From the opening of the country in 1853 to the Boshin War in 1868 and the Meiji period that followed, Japanese society underwent massive, but gradual, social, military, and economic reforms. Due to this, when the reform mechanic is enabled, not all troops are available from the start. Instead, better modern troops will gradually be unlocked over time either as the years pass or as the player's kingdom passes policies.

At the start of 1865, the Shogunate began a dedicated push to modernize their military. Beforehand, they had created the Sampeitai, or 'Three-Arms Corps', but that had been an unmitigated disaster. Prompted by the Kinmon Incident and Choshu's own civil war, the Shogunate's new reforms, forming units based on Samurai social rankings, ended in failure just as their previous ones had, but it started off the era of massive military reforms in Japan, which had been before isolated to a few small domains. These reforms unlock the Hoheitai and most of their equivalents, alongside units of unique organizations like the Mimawari-gumi and Shinsengumi.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Western Drill policy instead.

In 1866, something thought unthinkable occurred: the Shogunate lost a war against Choshu. The Second Choshu Expedition had been intended to remind Japan of the Bakufu's strength, and to deal with the rebellious domain once and for all. Instead, the 150,000 strong army of the Shogunate was routed by the 4000 men of Choshu and their modern rifles, losing thousands of men and inflicting only a few hundred casualties in return. With this failure, and the ascension of Tokugawa Yoshinobu as Shogun, Japan entered a furor of reform. Yoshinobu himself worked to reform the Bakufu army, establishing the Hoheitai, Yugekitai, and Denshutai, while many other domains were incentivized to adopt proper modernized infantry.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are mostly unlocked with the Standard Uniforms policy instead.

Emperor Komei had opposed the entirety of the outside world, advocating fiercely for Sonno-joi. However, his son was not so inflexible. Following Komei's death of smallpox in early 1867, the teenaged emperor and his advisors began a series of reforms of their own, establishing the new Imperial guard, while other pro-Imperial forces, such as the Jinshotai of Tosa, began coalescing into a modern army of their own. At the same time, Choshu began reforming their remaining Shotai militias into proper units of their own, in preparation for the turmoil everone knew was coming.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Standard Uniforms or Officer Academies policies instead.

Even as Japan reformed around them, many of the northernmost domains, as well as a few in Kansai, remained stagnant. The foolishness of this policy became apparent when the Boshin War broke out in early 1868, as the samurai of these domains suffered catastrophic defeats at the hands of peasants armed with modern rifles. These domains, most notable including Kubota on the Imperial side and Sendai on the Shogunate side, began to rapidly reorganize in an attempt to stave off defeat from those invading their domains.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Standard Uniforms or Western Drill policies instead.

While in essence the same as the {BOSHIN_REFORMS_LINK} in their timing and reasoning, Aizu domain took a rather unique approach to reforming their military. Still unwilling to allow peasants in their military, Aizu instead implemented their 4 Gods Organization, classifying the samurai of their domain into one of four units, based on age. The Byakkotai were the youngest, made up of 16-17 year olds, followed by the Suzakutai (18-35), Seiryutai (36-49), and the Genbutai (50+), alongside a number of volunteer units that sprung up across the domain. Ultimately, however, these units were not enough to stave off the invasion of their domain and brutal siege of their castle.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Western Drill policy instead.

Kishu domain, ruled by the Kishu Tokugawa, one of the Gosanke, or 'Three Noble Houses', of the Tokugawa Shogunate, reformed far later than most of Japan. Rather than taking inspiration from Britain or France like the rest of Japan, Kishu instead built their army along the Prussian model, implementing a conscript system that required a few years in active duty, then a few in the reserves, followed by service in the militia. However, these reforms occurred after the Boshin War, and ultimately came to naught as the Bakuhan system was dissolved and the private armies of the daimyo were folded into the new Imperial army.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Implement Conscription policy instead.

A small, final reform, this represents the units that were formed in the Meiji era, such as the Battotai or marines, that were added to the mod. While the time these units were created is somewhat outside the scope of the mod, and took place after these reforms actually happen, they were added into the game to fill their specific niches.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Implement Conscription policy instead.

The Caste Mechanic is an optional mechanic added in Bakumatsu to reflect the caste system of Edo period Japan. This caste system, put into place at the founding of the Tokugawa Shogunate, reflected the Tokugawa clan's deep paranoia and fear of being replaced. Due to this, it is often more of a restriction than a boon, and is not recommended if you want to enjoy a simple, easy playthrough.

To the merchants and businessmen of the outside world, the newly opened Japan was a goldmine. The price of gold and silver was cheaper than the rest of the world, and there was a huge market for outside products: most notably, firearms. Numerous arms dealers flocked to the archipelago, selling guns, uniforms, {FIELD_ARTILLERY_LINK}, and expertise in exchange for money and privileges. Found by walking around the keeps of any town, foreign merchants sell modern guns, artillery, and uniforms to the player. These wares each merchant offers differ by ethnicity. While all offer uniforms and antique flintlocks, British merchants offer the versatility of the many variants of the Enfield and Snider-Enfield rifles, alongside the best cannons, French merchants offer high quality rifles and cheap and light artillery, German merchants sell cheaper rifles, and American merchants sell all things repeating: revolvers, repeating rifles, and gatling guns.

Cannons weren't just used to siege fortresses anymore in the 19th century. Every modern military would field a battery of artillery, and heavy guns were worth their weight in gold in Bakumatsu era Japan. Pieces of field artillery can be purchased from {FOREIGN_MERCHANTS_LINK}, but are very expensive and very heavy, meaning that too many cannons will bankrupt even an endgame player and slow the party's progress to a crawl. To use these pieces in battle, you must have artillerist troops, marked by a cannon icon on their unit. You can only have 1 artillerist for every 10 men in your army, and can deploy a number of pieces equal to half your artillerists. These guns also start in your reserves when you start a siege, and will not be lost even if the deployed versions are destroyed.{newline}{newline}Artillery can be deployed while pressing K during the deployment phase

When using {FIELD_ARTILLERY_LINK}, each type of cannon has a default ammunition type, and a handful of special ammunition types. For example, the La Hitte Mountain Gun can shoot shells, round shot, or canister shot. For you or members of your party to be able to use specialized ammo in battle, the overall commander of your side in the battle must have the 'Stonecutters' or 'Siege Engineer' perk.{newline}{newline}You can switch ammo by hitting P before reloading the artillery in battle.

Kansai is the centermost region of Japan, and the origin of most strife in the Bakumatsu. Here sonno-joi radicals and shogunate loyalists clash in the streets of Kyoto and in the court of the Emperor. From here arose Tokugawa Iemochi, the current Shogun, and Ii Naosuke, the Tairo who dominated the Bakufu throughout the period until his assassination in 1860. The domains of Kansai were once some of the strongest for the Shogun, but many are being pushed away by their political rivals, forcing them into joining the Imperial cause.

Tōhoku, the northernmost region of Honshū, was the home of the last holdouts of the Shogunate cause in the Boshin war. The domains here are some of the oldest and most entrenched in Japan, with clans such as the Date of Sendai, the Nanbu of Morioka, and the Tsugaru of Hirosaki having ruled in the same region for centuries. Tōhoku, due to its isolation, is also fairly conservative. Few domains have truly begun reforming, leaving them far behind the rapidly modernizing domains of the southwest.

Shikoku maintains a more cautious stance than the rest of Japan. With very few large domains, the island is almost entirely dominated by the Yamauchi of Tosa and the Hachisuka of Tokushima, as well as the Date of Uwajima, a cousin of the larger main house in Sendai. Even so, these few domains are tiny compared to some of the mighty domains in the rest of Japan. The samurai of Shikoku have flocked to the sonno-joi cause en masse, much to the dismay of the more pro-Shogunate daimyo of their domains, and internal conflicts have begun to tear them apart.

Kyūshū is the core of Japan's reform in the Bakumatsu. Due to its isolation at the southwest of Japan, the island remained largely untouched by the Tokugawa when they founded the Bakufu, leaving the island largely under the control of powerful tozama daimyo, like the Shimazu of Satsuma, the Nabeshima of Saga, and the Hosokawa of Kumamoto. As the Shogun's authority continues to wane, the daimyo of Kyūshū have seen their chance, rapidly rearming with modern weapons in the hopes of becoming the dominant power in this new era.

Chūgoku, stretching across western Honshū, has become one of the most unstable regions of Japan in the Bakumatsu. Once a stronghold of loyalist domains guarding the western approaches to the capital, the region is now defined by upheaval and rebellion, chiefly in Chōshū, whose radical samurai and reformist leadership openly defy the Bakufu, clashing repeatedly with shogunate forces and other loyal domains. Neighboring territories such as Hiroshima and Okayama have been drawn into the turmoil, and Chūgoku is becoming the spark that will light the fire of war.

Kantō is the heart of the Shogunate. Within it is Edo, the capital of the Bakufu, and in which all daimyo were required to live in off years until 1862. Despite that, the region is not as stable as the Shogun wishes it to be. The samurai of Mito, ruled by one of the chief branches of the Tokugawa, are fierce advocates of expelling the foreign barbarians, a stance that the Shogunate is unable to take, leading to constant agitation and the ongoing Mito rebellion. Even so, the region remains loyal to the Tokugawa, with even the Mito samurai wishing to reform, rather than overthrow the Shogunate.

Tōkai, stretching along the southern coast, is the home of the Tōkaidō, the most important of the Five Routes that link Edo to the rest of central Honshū. The Tōkaidō specifically links Edo and Kyoto, and is vital for maintaining the Shogun's control of the Imperial Court. Tōkai is almost entirely Tenryō land, alongside a handful of smaller Fudai domains, with the sole large domain being the Tokugawa branch in Owari. These domains largely remain loyal to the Shogun, but will be some of the first to roll over against the Imperial forces when they marched to Edo.

Tōsan, the mountainous heart of central Japan, is highly conservative. Made up almost entirely of Tenryō land and a handful of Fudai daimyo, Tōsan has no great lords of their own, leading to their growing irrelavance in this period, as the powerful daimyo in the fringes of Japan increasingly dominate politics. Even so, Tōsan is vital to the Shogunate's continued dominance, providing a great deal of their manpower and influence.

Ezo (modern Hokkaidō), home to the Ainu, remained a remote frontier. In the late Bakumatsu, the Matsumae Domain managed small garrisons and fortified trading posts to assert shogunate influence, while Ainu communities maintained autonomous governance. The region was a delicate frontier where indigenous autonomy, limited shogunate oversight, and foreign concerns, particularly Russian encroachment, intersected.

The Tozama are 'outside' lords who, although they submit to the Tokugawa after the decisive battles that establish shogunal supremacy, maintain control over large, semi-autonomous domains and wield considerable local power, wealth, and military strength, yet their political influence within the inner councils of the shogunate remains limited, forcing them to act cautiously and independently in matters of national importance. Their position allows them to preserve strong local authority and maintain sizable, loyal armies, making them capable of both defending their interests and exerting pressure when opportunities arise, but always under the shadow of Tokugawa oversight and exclusion from key decision-making.

The Fudai are hereditary vassals of the Tokugawa who enjoy long-standing trust and occupy critical administrative and military roles within the shogunate, overseeing strategically located domains that, while often smaller in size, provide essential political and military leverage to maintain the Tokugawa order; their loyalty is relied upon to enforce shogunal policies and manage affairs across the country, giving them consistent access to influence and power, yet they remain tightly constrained by the carefully maintained balance of authority that the shogunate imposes to prevent any one ally from becoming too dominant.

Tosa dominates southern Shikoku, a land of steep mountains and sheltered valleys that have allowed the Yamauchi clan to cultivate a tradition of independence. The domain produces politically active samurai and reformist thinkers, who travel to Kyoto and Edo to debate modernization and imperial loyalty. Rivers carry lumber and silk to coastal ports, linking the inland valleys to trade networks. When disputes flare between coastal and inland powers, Tosa's samurai are quick to act, using both diplomacy and force to advance the clan's interests.

Spread across river valleys and rugged hills, Morioka has been the seat of the Nanbu clan for centuries. The domain's winters are harsh, but its villages and fortified towns reflect careful planning and resilience. Morioka's samurai maintain long-standing martial traditions, while the local economy depends on a mix of agriculture and horse breeding. Centuries of governance have forged a community where survival and endurance shape both politics and everyday life.

Hirosaki, perched near the northern tip of Honshu, is defined as much by its rivalry with Morioka as by its own lands. The Tsugaru clan governs fertile plains crossed by rivers, supporting villages and castle towns that thrive despite the harsh climate. Its samurai are fewer than Morioka's but disciplined, and the domain often shifts alliances to avoid being dominated by neighbors. Festivals, shrines, and the rhythms of local life give Hirosaki a cultural identity distinct from its northern rivals.

Kubota stretches across the northern plains toward the Sea of Japan, where the Satake clan balances tradition with pragmatism. Its winters are bitter, but the land yields rice and supports horse breeding, sustaining both townspeople and samurai. The domain is famous for retaining the old ways: its warriors are said to be the last in Japan to fight fully armored. Though deeply conservative, Kubota leans toward the imperial cause, guided by practical concerns rather than ideology, blending old martial habits with careful political calculation.

Shonai occupies a long strip along the Sea of Japan, where fertile farmland and maritime trade enrich the Sakai clan. Unlike many northern neighbors, Shonai adapts quickly, modernizing weapons and training without abandoning its traditions. Its castle towns hum with commerce, and local craftsmanship flourishes alongside the growing military reforms. The domain's leaders remain deeply loyal to the shogunate, yet their readiness and organization make Shonai one of the most capable forces in the north.

Sprawling across southern Tōhoku, Sendai has been shaped over generations by the Date clan. Rivers, plains, and rolling hills support large towns and productive farms, while fortified castles reflect the clan's long martial history. Sendai's culture values practical governance and education, and samurai numbers are substantial. Politically, the domain remains loyal to the shogunate, but the leadership watches events in the southwest closely, balancing caution with preparation for change.

Yonezawa is a smaller, mountainous domain under the Uesugi clan, with a history of careful stewardship after past losses. Its towns cling to hillsides and valleys, sustaining a tight-knit community of farmers and samurai. Local culture emphasizes tradition, efficiency, and scholarly pursuits, and the samurai are respected as much for their administrative skill as for martial ability. Politically, Yonezawa treads carefully, maintaining loyalty while watching the ambitions of larger neighbors.

Nestled in the mountains of southern Tōhoku, Aizu has long been a fortress of the Tokugawa. Its river valleys support fertile rice fields, while dense forests provide timber and fuel for the region's castles and towns. Generations of Matsudaira rulers shaped the domain into a stronghold of martial tradition, where warriors trained from youth and the people prized honor and duty. Temples, local crafts, and educational institutions thrive alongside military life, giving Aizu a culture both disciplined and deeply rooted in centuries of history.

Ozu sits on the western coast of Shikoku, where rocky shores and sheltered bays shape both life and defense. The Katō clan governs a domain where fishing, salt production, and local trade sustain towns and samurai alike. Its castle overlooks the sea, a reminder of past conflicts and the domain's reliance on maritime knowledge. Ozu values prudence and order, blending coastal commerce with disciplined administration to maintain stability in a small but tightly organized domain.

Iwo-Matsuyama, ruled by the Matsudaira clan, occupies a coastal and mountainous region of Shikoku, where fertile river valleys meet rocky hills. Its towns are modest but well-organized, with local markets supporting both farmers and samurai households. The domain has a long history of managing these challenging lands, emphasizing careful administration and fortification rather than sheer military strength. While its samurai maintain traditional martial training, the domain also leans on commerce, fishing, and regional trade to sustain its people.

Uwajima domain is led by a branch of the Date clan, located far from their homeland in Sendai. During the Bakumatsu period, their Daimyo, Date Munenari, was considered one of the Four Wise Lords of the Bakumatsu, alongside Yamauchi Toyoshige, Shimazu Nariakira, and Matsudaira Yoshinaga. During the Bakumatsu, they remained neutral, acting as a go between between the two sides, a stance which ultimately left them less relevant in the Meiji era.

Tokushima Domain, despite their strong connections to the Shogunate, remained neutral during the Bakumatsu. Instead of supporting the Shogun or Emperor, they advocated for the kōbu gattai movement, which proposed the unification of the Imperial court and Shogunate against the western powers. Even so, many Tokushima samurai were rather radically pro-Imperial.

The capital in name of Japan, Kyoto is the seat of the Emperor. Once the power center of Japan, its decline during the late Sengoku period and throughout the Edo period have left the city a shell of its former self. However, the turmoil of the Bakumatsu has brought the city back to relevance, as Daimyo clash in the halls of government and samurai and ronin clash in the streets of the city.

Hikone sits along the shores of Lake Biwa, dominated by its sprawling castle and the Ii clan, whose samurai are famous for their bright red armor and fierce discipline. The Ii have long been loyal to the Tokugawa, serving as both military leaders and administrators of the shogunate. The assassination of Ii Naosuke sent shockwaves through the domain, and his retainers seethe with outrage against the Sonno-joi movement.

Ruled by the Hisamatsu Matsudaira, the Kuwana domain is fiercely loyal to the Shogunate, with members of the domain fighting through the end of the war in the North and in Ezo. During the war, their soldiers will be some of the best trained and drilled among all the Shogunate troops.

Kishu, alternatively named Kii or Wakayama, is a powerful shinpan domain and the fifth richest domain in Japan. It is ruled by one of the three Gosanke houses, descendants of Tokugawa Ieyasu who exist as backups in case the main Tokugawa line ever falters. Despite providing the current Shogun, Iemochi, Kishu domain will go on to surrender to and join the Imperial side

Rising out of humble roots, Tsu domain was founded by Todo Takatora, a low ranking ashigaru who later became a daimyo under Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Oda Nobunaga. Due to their loyalty to the Shogunate, samurai in the Edo period often state that 'If the battle occurs, the vanguard is the Hikone's Ii clan and the Todo clan of Ise.'

The location of the main branch of the Yuki Matsudaira, Fukui-han is a wealthy modernized domain. In the 1850s, they instituted one of the first vaccination programs in Japan, and they've modernized their military, phasing out their archery corps in favor of riflemen. Their lord had an eye for talent, with statesmen like Yokoi Shōnan, Hashimoto Sanai and Yuri Kimimasa rising out of Fukui.

Nagaoka is far more modernized than most Shogunate domains, reforming under the leadership of Kawai Tsugunosuke. Nagaoka is the rare exception to the northern refusal to modernize, being one of the few domains in Hokuriku and Tohoku to fully modernize, at one point owning 2/3 of the Gatling Guns in Japan.

Kaga Domain stretches across Hokuriku, a land of fertile plains, bustling towns, and the glittering rivers that feed into the Sea of Japan. The Maeda clan has ruled for generations, amassing wealth that rivals even the shogunate in scale, and even their lesser retainers are as wealthy as Daimyo. However, Kaga is also deeply unwilling to reform, for fear of being targetted by the Shogunate.

Obama Domain hugs the northern coast of Wakasa Bay, where the town's harbor has long connected the mountains to the sea. The Sakai clan rules here with a careful hand, balancing the needs of merchants, fishermen, and samurai. The domain is known for its skilled boatmen and fortified castle that watches over both river traffic and coastal approaches.

A fairly new and small domain, Jozai is highly loyal to the Shogunate. They would fight throughout the entire war, only surrendering upon hearing that the Shogun would keep a fief after the war. Jozai was one of only two domains to be stripped of their holdings during the Boshin war.

Owari is ruled by the seniormost of the Gosanke of the Tokugawa. Owari-han is a powerful and wealthy domain, behind only the Kaga, Satsuma, and Sendai domains, and the most powerful of the Tokugawa houses besides the Shogunate itself. Despite their family ties, however, Owari would go on to support the Imperial forces during the Boshin War.

Despite being ruled by one of the Gosanke of the Tokugawa, Mito Domain is a hotbed of Sonno-joi and anti-Shogunate sentiment in the Bakumatsu. Throughout this period, agitators from Mito constantly undermine the Shogunate and push other domains to adopt the ideology. While not as influential as Satsuma and Choshu would come to be, it cannot be denied that Mito was one of the cores of the Sonno-joi.

The Tokugawa may be the Shoguns, but they are also daimyo. At its core, the Bakufu is simply a domain so powerful that all others must bow to it. This power is maintained via Tenryo, land directly under the control of the Tokugawa. Containing some of the wealthiest cities and areas of Japan, most of Tokai, Tosan, and Kanto was Tenryo, as was significant chunks of Kyushu, Chugoku, and Kansai.

No city in Japan is greater than Edo, the seat of the Shogunate. From here reign the Tokugawa shoguns, and it is here that over one million people live in the peace that is the Edo period. The center of Japan in many ways, Edo is the center of culture, administration, the economy, and the military. The influence it had upon Japan in this period cannot be overstated, and it is here that the deals and alliances that led to the fall of the Bakufu were formed.

Chōshū occupies the western tip of Honshu, with rugged mountains and jagged coasts that have long shaped the character of its people. The Mōri clan has ruled here for generations, cultivating a culture of fierce independence and hatred of the Shogunate. Samurai from Chōshū are known for their sharp swords, quick thinking, and readiness to defy authority when necessary. In recent years, Choshu has emerged as a hotbed of political action, containing many of the most radical ishin shishi in Japan.

Hiroshima Domain sprawls across the fertile delta of the Ota River, with the castle town at its center serving as both administrative hub and cultural heart. The Asano clan has ruled here for generations, known for disciplined samurai and a stable, well-organized administration. The domain has long fostered artisans, merchants, and schools, giving it a reputation for both martial and cultural refinement. Politically, Hiroshima maintains a careful balance: its samurai enforce order and support the shogunate when called upon, but the radicals of Choshu force them further towards the sonno-joi side.

Tottori-han, ruled by the Ikeda, has long been close with the Shogunate. Their daimyo are allowed to use the Matsudaira name and crest, they have the right to carry their swords into Edo castle, and their daimyo is the half brother of the man who will one day become the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu. However, they also have many proponents of the Imperial cause within, and just the year ago a pro-Imperial samurai assassinated a pro-Shogunate official within their domain.

One of the few Tozama daimyo to serve under the Shogunate, the Ikeda of Okayama domain are relatively sonno-joi, but still support the Shogunate. During the Boshin War, seeing the threat, the daimyo adopted a more pro-imperial successor and retired, so as to allow the domain to take the winning side without violating his own beliefs. While the domain itself avoided joining the war, many units formed in the domain would go fight in the north.

Kurume domain is a fierce battleground between Sonno-Joi and Shogunate supporters, both originating from the Tenpo School. Following the death of Arima Yorinaga in 1846, they split into the Gai-doshi, a radical sonno-joi traditionalist faction, and Nai-doshi, a reformer, pro-western, pro-shogunate factions. Currently, the Nai-doshi hold sway, but who knows if that will change.

One of the wealthiest domains in Japan, Kumamoto is ruled by the Hosokawa clan, one of the most powerful clans in Japan. They are more hesitant to join the Emperor than many of the more radical domains, but are still a powerful modern domain.

Nestled in the valleys of southern Kyushu, Hitoyoshi is a small but proud domain, its hills and rivers shaping life as much as the Sagara clan that rules it. Their samurai, like so many others in the period, are deeply split between the Shogunate and Emperor, leading to their own internal clashes.

Fukuoka is very prominently Sonno-joi, so much so that the Shogunate is considering arresting their daimyo on suspicion of rebellion. However, they are unwilling to actually dedicate their own troops to the cause, instead using forces they consider expendable, cobbled together from what the dregs of society to war against the Shogunate.

Kokura is the rare Shogunate loyalist in the southwest, supporting the Shogun even despite being surrounded by larger, more pro-Imperial domains. This attitude remains ever despite losses against the sonno-joi forces, an almost admirable attitude if it didn't end up with a burning castle.

Saga is perhaps the most modern domain in Japan. The Nabeshima have invested in steam engines, steel refining, artillery, and modern firearms, alongside vaccination programs and significant domain reforms, modernizing even before the Black Ships arrived in 1853. There are few domains friendlier to the west than Saga.

Satsuma occupies a unique position in the late Bakumatsu. The Shimazu joined the shogunate under their own terms due to their distance from the rest of Japan and their military power, providing them with a semi-independent status. The domain is highly militarized, with more samurai than any other domain in Japan, and samurai renowned for their loyalty, identifying first as Satsuma men before anything else. They are also rapidly reforming, forming some of the most modern troops in Japan.

Strategically located in the westernmost part of the San'yō region, near the Kanmon Straits that separate Honshu from Kyushu, Kushizaki is a port castle town originally by the Naitō clan, from which it is possible to control the sea and the flow of trade and people across the western provinces.

Positioned near the confluence of several key trade routes in the Chūgoku region, the castle town of Sanbonmatsu has become a target for expanding warlords. While its military importance seems negligible, its location along vital supply routes makes it a key target for forces looking to consolidate control over the region.

Originally built as a small fortified residence for the Mōri clan this coastal castle town grew in importance along with the expansion of its inhabitants' power, while its hilltop location ensures control over the surrounding territories and sea routes.

Iwami is famed for its rich silver mines, which have made it one of the most valuable settlements in Japan. The most powerful daimyos of the region have long battled for control of the Iwami ginzan, which has most recently fallen to the Mōri clan.

Gassantoda is a castle town in San'in that traces its origins back to the Kamakura period and before that to the Heian period when a fortress was built to protect trade routes and the renowned local steel production. More recently, Gassantoda became the stage for the last stand of the once dominant Amago clan against the ascendant Ōuchi and Mōri clans, with the conquest by Mōri Motonari marking the definitive shift of power in the region.

Okayama is a castle town located in the western part of the Chūgoku region, providing both military and economic advantages through access to maritime trade routes and strategic passage between Honshu and Shikoku

Ichijodani is a fortified town in western Hokuriku, surrounded on all sides by the natural defences of rivers and mountains, making it a difficult target for any besieger. Built by the Asakura clan, Ichijodani has grown into a centre of culture, craftsmanship and religion thanks to the hospitality afforded by the Asakura clan to refugees fleeing Kyoto during the Ōnin War, making it a jewel rivaling the Imperial Capital itself.

Originally a fortified temple complex of the Kaga Ikko movement, Oyama has evolved into a significant stronghold in the Hokuriku region and its strategic and religious value has drawn the attention of powerful neighbors.

A Nanao, the stronghold of the Hatakeyama clan, is one of the most important castle towns along the Noto Peninsula. Surrounded by mountains and the sea, its defenses are strong, and its harbor allows for active maritime trade.

Perched atop a steep mountain, the castle town of Kasugayama was originally a possession of the Nagao clan, but has served as the seat of the powerful Uesugi clan since Uesugi Kenshin, born a Nagao,  took over. Kenshin turned Kasugayama into a center of military power in Echigo from which he departed several times at the head of his armies to challenge the Takeda clan.

Situated on the coast of Echigo Province, Niigata is a prosperous port town benefiting from maritime trade and fertile agricultural lands. The Shinano River provides an essential route for transporting rice and goods inland. The town falls under the influence of Uesugi Kenshin, whose strong rule ensures stability in the region. Fishermen, salt merchants, and shipbuilders contribute to Niigata’s economy, making it an important asset for Kenshin’s war efforts.

Fukashi is a castle town built amongst the mountains of Shinano to protect the domains of the Ogasawara clan until it was taken over by its parent clan following a famous siege by Takeda Shingen, who subsequently converted it into one of the outposts of the expanding Takeda clan.

Kōfu, a castle town in the heart of Kai Province in the southern part of the Tōsan region, has been the home of the Takena clan since its beginnings, but has only recently grown considerably thanks to Takeda Shingen, who has made it the centre of his expanding domain and undertaken major flood control projects to increase agricultural production and quality of life

Sunpu has served as the seat of the powerful Imagawa clan for decades, during which the castle town has flourished as a center of governance, trade and culture, benefiting from its location along the strategic Tōkaidō road. However, the Imagawa’s power has declined significantly since their crushing defeat at the hands of Oda Nobunaga exposing Sunpu and other Imagawa domains to the thirst for conquest of neighbouring lords.

Hamamatsu is a castle town in Tokai, built by the Imagawa clan to guard the access the access to the vital Tōkaidō highway, it was then taken over by the rising Tokugawa Ieyasu in the aftermath of the battle of Okehazama.

Okazaki, the birthplace of the rising lord Tokugawa Ieyasu, is a vital castle town in Mikawa Province. Under Tokugawa rule, it has been reinforced as a military base, securing the clan’s control over the region. The castle town is flourishing, with a growing population of samurai, merchants, and craftsmen. Its position along the Tōkaidō road makes it an essential stop for travelers and military movements.

Built in the Kamakura period to guard the highways between Kyoto and the Shogunal capital, Kiyosu has long been the seat of the Oda clan of Owari and the site of political intrigue and military conflicts surrounding the clan, at least until the young lord Oda Nobunaga chose to move his seat to Gifu. Although the relocation of the court weakened its position, Kiyosu remains an important fortified city bustling with activity.

Hidden deep within the mountainous interior of the Tosan region, Sakurabora has long served as the fortified residence of the Anekouji, guarding key approaches into central Japan. Its elevated position offers commanding views of the rugged valleys below, making it a valuable asset in controlling travel and communication through the region.

“The one who controls Gifu controls Japan” is a common saying that emphasises the strategic location of this castle town. Once a possession of the Saitō clan and recently seized by Oda Nobunaga, who chose to rename it after the legendary mountain where most of ancient china was unified and the birthplace of Confucious, signalling to everyone his intention to unify the whole of Japan.

A Odawara, the stronghold of the powerful Hojo clan, stands as an impregnable fortress in the Kanto region. With its vast network of walls, moats, and outlying fortifications, it is considered one of the most well-defended castles in Japan. The city below is a thriving center of trade, with merchants, farmers, and artisans benefiting from Hojo governance. Odawara’s strategic location allows the Hojo to control access to eastern Japan, ensuring their dominance over the region.

Originally developed from a small fishing village as a fortified residence for a local noble of the Heian Period, Edo was later fortified to become the castle town that currently towers over the Musashino Plateau and Edo Bay. The recent turmoil in Kantō has seen Edo shift between the different warring Clans and has severely hampered its development, but the city still retains its enormous potential.

Originally the seat of the namesake clan, Ota is a castle town in Kantō in close proximity to the vital Tōkaidō road, which connects the region to the capital Kyoto, making it an important military and administrative center.

First built in the Heian period,  the castle town of Utsunomiya was the seat of the clan of the same name for centuries and one of the most important centres in the Kantō region which exerts control over many of the local land routes.

Built as the fortified residence of the Nagano clan, the castle town of Minowa has long been a critical stronghold for the control of the surrounding region, which made it a mandatory target in the confrontation between the Uesugi and Takeda clans, until the forces of Takeda Shingen seized Minowa resulting in the demise of the Nagano clan and the death of all its members.

Himeji was originally built in the early Muromachi period by the Akamatsu clan as a small fortified outpost atop Himeyama Hill and along the western route to capital Kyoto, but underwent several demolitions and reconstructions until it reached its present form as a mighty castle town barring the way to would-be invaders.

Dominated by the temple fortress of Ishiyama Hongan-ji, Osaka has grown into a major center of religious and economic activity. The temple fortress, controlled by the militant Ikkō-ikki, serves as the stronghold of the Jōdo Shinshū sect, resisting the rule of samurai warlords.

Sakai, one of the wealthiest and most autonomous cities in Japan, thrives as a center of commerce. The city’s merchant guilds operate independently of the warring daimyōs, maintaining direct trade with China and Portuguese traders. Famous for its high-quality firearms, swords, and luxury goods, Sakai’s economy flourishes even as war ravages the surrounding regions.

Once the great imperial capital of Japan, Nara remains a center of Buddhist influence and cultural heritage. The massive temples of Tōdaiji and Kōfukuji stand as reminders of its former glory, housing powerful monastic factions.

Kyoto, once the unrivaled capital of Japan, emerged almost completely destroyed by the struggles for control over the central power. The authority of the Ashikaga Shogunate has crumbled, leaving the city at the mercy of the warring daimyos, while the Imperial Court sits back and watches helplessly. Nevertheless, Kyoto remains the depository of secular traditions and while its days as the true centre of power seem to be over, its religious and cultural influence persists.

A seemingly quiet castle town built atop Mount Kinugasa, Kannonji has been repeatedly embroiled in the conflicts of its ancestral owners, the Rokkaku clan, and only the castle’s natural defenses have allowed it to resist several sieges.

Built as the fortified seat of the Azai clan to rule over the surrounding region, the castle town of Odani sits atop a steep ridge, its defenses making it a formidable stronghold, while its position along key trade routes ensure the growing prosperity of the settlement.
Koyama is strategic stronghold in Southern Kyushu, nestled in the rugged terrain of Higo Province, where mountain passes connect inland domains to the western coast.

A small but strategically located settlement, Uchi serves as a waypoint for travelers and merchants moving through its province. The town’s location makes it valuable to any daimyo seeking control over the surrounding region.

The castle town of Sadowara, located in the southern portion of Kyushu, has served as the seat of the Itō clan for generations. Benefiting from fertile plains and proximity to maritime routes, Sadowara has flourished as both an administrative and agricultural center becoming the epicenter of the Itō clan's expansion attempts in the region.

A castle town nestled deep in the mountains of South-western Kyushu, Hitoyoshi has served as the seat of the Sagara clan since the Kamakura period. It is said that during the construction work a moon-shaped stone was unearthed, thus giving rise to the alternative folk name of moon castle. Popular tales aside, Hitoyoshi stands as an imposing fortification that has only once been attacked by an enemy and with a fatal outcome.

Benefiting from its position along key maritime trade routes and its proximity to the island’s northern provinces, Nyushima has grown into a prosperous castle town, also thanks to the influence of the Ōtomo clan, that has promoted the town as a center of local governance.

Nestled within the rugged highlands of northern Kyushu, Kiidani has long served as a fortified settlement, guarding the access to the western island of Japan. Its position overlooking vital inland routes has given it strategic relevance amid the growing contest for control over Kyushu and has already turned Kiidani into a conflict point between the Ouchi and Otomo in the past.

Located in north-western Kyushu, Yanagawa is strategically located on the banks of the Chikugo River, at the crossroads of trade routes connecting much of the region, which facilitates both trade and military movements.

Well-positioned between coastal trade routes and mountain strongholds of western Kyushu, Kumamoto has enjoyed steady growth thanks to the flow of trade and local production that made it a thriving and well-defended castle town.

Perched on a prominent hill in northern Kyushu, Tachibanayama was originally built for its namesake Tachibana clan as a fortified town, whose control over the surrounding areas remains vital for securing key trade routes and access to both land and sea.

Muranaka has long served as a local stronghold in Western Kyushu, functioning as a minor seat of governance under the protection of the Aso clan, whose authority once extended across the central highlands. With the Aso clan’s power sharply declined under pressure from the Shimazu to the south and the Ōtomo to the east, Muranaka is now left vulnerable.

The castle town of Hinoe sits on the west coast of Kyushu on the Shimabara Peninsula. Built in the early Kamakura period, Hinoe has since served as the home base and major source of profits for the Arima clan, who from here controlled maritime trade routes and more recently the Nanban foreign trade.
Nakamura, is a castle town in Western Shikoku. Surrounded by rivers and mountains, it enjoys a natural defensive advantage, benefitting from the fertile lands that produce rice and timber.
Located in the inland reaches of Shikoku, Kurose is a strategically placed castle town that provides control over the inland routes and a valuable defensive position against neighbouring domains.

Yuzuki is a fortified port town in western Shikoku, built by the Kōno clan as as a gateway to maritime commerce. Despite its modest size, Yuzuki has prospered thanks to the Kōno clan's unofficial alliance with local pirates and the castle's defensive position.

Okou is a castle town located in a a key strategic location in the southern part of Shikoku, that has been serving as the ancestral seat of the Chōsokabe clan since the Kamakura period. Okou recently played a crucial role in the consolidation of power by Chōsokabe Motochika.

Amagiri is a fortified town on top of the namesake Mountain, built by the Kagawa Clan as its seat in the Northern part of Shikoku. Thanks to its strategically fortified location and access to the Inland Sea coast, Amagiri is an important centre for controlling the surrounding territory and trade routes.

Ushiki is a castle town in eastern Kyushu built by the Daimyo Ōtomo Sōrin as the main base for his expanding domain. Located on what is virtually an island connected to the rest of Kyushu only during low tides, Ushiki dominates the eponymous bay.

The castle town of Kurokawa was built by the Ashina clan as its seat in the southernmost part of Ōu region, an isolated area that ensured that Kurokawa could grow while avoiding the worst of the conflicts between neighbouring lords.

Built during the Kamakura period, the castle town of Yonezawa has served as the seat of the Date clan since they drove out the previous lords and from here they plan the domination of neighbouring domains.

Yamagata has been the seat of the Mogami since before they adopted this name, its location marked by the many mountains and rivers that shield it and at the same time make it an important connection centre for the surrounding regions.

Ishinomaki is a bustling coastal town in the southern part of the Ōu region that has grown as an important port for trade and fishing as Matsushima Bay provides natural protection and  the Kitakami River serves as a vital route for transporting goods inland. Although its strategic location has ensured its prosperity, it also makes it an important military target for the plans of expansion of the local clans.

Sakata is a a key port in the northern part of the Tōhoku region, the castle town has grown into a vital hub for trade, particularly due to its access to the Sea of Japan and its proximity to the rich agricultural lands of the surrounding region.

Situated along the windswept coastline of northern Honshu, Tzuchizaki‑Minato has long served as a crucial point for maritime trade and the transport of goods between the main islands and the northern provinces.
Located along a key mountain pass, Sannohoe is a fortified town that serves as a military outpost, guarding vital routes for trade and troop movements on the borders of competing powers.

Located in the northernmost reaches of Honshu, Tosaminato serves as a key trade hub with the Ainu people of Hokkaido although the harsh winters and isolation make it difficult to defend, leaving it vulnerable to raids. Once a thriving port and administrative center of the Andō clan, Tosaminato has declined following the clan’s expulsion.

I can share my story with you, if you have the time.

I served a small fudai domain for twelve years. My lord was a decent man, but his chief councillors were parasites who spent more time arguing over stipends than preparing for the storm that is coming.

When Commodore Perry arrived, I said we should modernize our troops. When Choshu began arming with Western weapons, I said we should do the same. They called me reckless. Then they bought rifles themselves and pretended it had been their idea all along.
I spoke too openly in council. Now I travel without a stipend, without a master, and without patience for men who mistake caution for wisdom.
How virtue has crumbled since the old days.
At any rate, I'll fight for any man willing to take the same risks that his men face.
I have not betrayed my lord. I merely refused to flatter fools.
You know, you'd think this place could serve proper sake, instead of this piss... Sorry, where were we? Ah yes, my story.
I was born the son of a village headman, but I studied in a domain school where the teachers spoke of loyalty to the Throne and the corruption of Edo.
The Shogunate signs treaties with foreigners, bows to foreign demands, and allows foreign ships into our waters. Every year the old order grows weaker, yet the officials tell us to remain calm.
I have not joined any conspiracy. Not yet. But if a man truly intends to restore honor to the realm, I would hear him out before I hear another speech from a Tokugawa bureaucrat.
Aye, real honor is as scarce as hen's teeth these days.
A disappointing thing, that so few are willing to die for His Imperial Majesty.
Let me tell you something - I'm sick of cowardice, sick of those who don't come forth to serve their Emperor.
The Emperor sits in Kyoto while weak men rule in his name.
You're a nosy one, I see.
I served with a patrol force outside Osaka. We escorted tax shipments, guarded roads, and kept hot-headed young samurai from turning every argument into a blood feud.
These days everyone talks about restoring this or expelling that. Fine words. But when merchants are robbed and villages burn, it is still Tokugawa officials who restore order.
The Shogunate is imperfect. So is every government ever created by men. I have no love for corrupt magistrates, but I fear chaos more than I fear reformers.
No doubt a sad state of affairs. So what do you do?
What? Does no one respect their lords anymore?
The Shogunate will stand with or without me. It has reigned for 250 years, and it will undoubtedly rule for another 1000.
Everyone complains about Edo until bandits appear on the road.
Refill my glass and I'll tell you.
A younger son of a samurai family, I was sent to Edo to study at a famous d┼ìj┼ì. Every evening the students argued politics more fiercely than they crossed swords.
Some swore the Emperor must rule directly. Others said the Tokugawa alone kept the peace. I came to master the blade, not speeches.
After too many duels over matters that had nothing to do with technique, I left. Steel cuts the same no matter whose crest is painted on the scabbard.
Indeed. Nobody is more important than a skilled swordsman.
Resentment is poison to a friendship. Men must learn to follow the natural flow.
I studied the sword to perfect myself. Now everyone wants me to choose a side.

My father traded through Nagasaki, where I first saw Dutch books, foreign instruments, and machines unlike anything made in Japan. While other boys practiced the sword, I struggled through foreign texts, determined to understand the secrets they contained.
The more I learned, the clearer it became that the outside world was changing faster than we were. Some say Western knowledge is poison. Others worship it without question. I think both are fools.

I do not seek to make Japan into the West. I only wish to learn whatever can strengthen her. So I travel where knowledge can be found, serving any lord wise enough to value skill over tradition alone.
Ah, the old days. And no doubt back then they complained about the older days. I've heard enough.

Well, I can't just sit around and drink myself to death, so I sell my sword to anyone worth following. I'm a good trainer - I don't bother with horsemen or archers, but if you've got good steady footmen I can do a lot with them.
Most men think the world ends at Japan's shores. I know better.
It's not many who ask that question.

I spent years riding between castle towns carrying my lord's messages. Most were dullΓÇötax records, supply requests, invitations to banquetsΓÇöbut now and then I was entrusted with letters sealed so tightly that men would kill to read them. I never broke a seal. I never asked questions. A messenger who lives long learns when not to be curious.

Still, it was impossible not to notice the country changing. Every road carried more soldiers than merchants. Every castle wanted rifles, powder, or foreign books. Men who smiled at one another in spring refused to speak by autumn.
When my lord died, his heir dismissed half the household to save money. I kept my horse and my knowledge of the roads. Those have served me better than any official seal ever did.
What? Does no one respect messengers anymore?
Well, I can't just sit around and drink myself to death, so I sell my sword to anyone worth following. I'm a good scout, anything you want me to find I will.
If you carry enough letters, you begin to understand the people who write them.

The Saigō are not daimyō, but few wield as much influence in Satsuma as Saigō Takamori. A samurai of humble origin and towering presence, Saigō is a leading voice in the sonnō jōi movement. Beloved by the lower samurai and feared by political rivals, he walks a tightrope between personal loyalty to the Shimazu clan and his growing vision for a reformed Japan. In 1864, Saigō has returned from exile to help Satsuma crush the Chōshū rebellion, but his heart lies with imperial cause. Torn between duty and destiny, the Saigō family rises not through land or armies, but through the charisma and ideals of its reluctant champion.

Hailing from a modest samurai background in Kagoshima, the Ōkubo are bureaucrats rather than warriors—but it is in politics that they sharpen their blades. Ōkubo Toshimichi, pragmatic and sharp-tongued, is fast becoming one of the most feared minds in Satsuma. A staunch ally of Saigō Takamori, he believes that only radical reform can save Japan from subjugation by the West. While others cry for war against foreign powers, Ōkubo sees the greater enemy in Japan's own corruption and feudal stagnation. As the Satsuma domain balances on the edge of rebellion, the Ōkubo clan builds networks, forges alliances, and prepares to steer the storm. In 1864, they are the hidden hand guiding the future of a crumbling shogunate.

The Kinno-to are violent Imperialists, called terrorists by some. Drawn from the ranks of the Shishi, their cause combines fierce reverence for the throne with violent action, embracing assassination, agitation, and open rebellion.
The Tenchūgumi are a small band of imperial loyalists who launched an armed uprising in Yamato in 1863, believing they are carrying out heaven's punishment against enemies of the emperor.

The Shinchōgumi are a Bakumatsu policing corps formed by the shogunate in Edo, composed mainly of loyalist rōnin tasked with patrols, guard duty, and keeping order in the capital as tensions with imperial forces grow. In 1864, they fell under the command of Shonai-han

Kameyama Shachū is a small, semi-private maritime venture founded by Sakamoto Ryōma to move weapons, conduct trade, and operate ships independent of the Bakufu. It will later evolve into the Kaientai, a more organized naval-style volunteer corps that carries out transport, escort, and political missions during the final years of the Bakumatsu.

The Aizu Joshigun are groups of Aizu domain women who organized themselves during the Boshin War, taking on support roles and, in many cases, joining combat alongside the domain's remaining defenders.

The Shōgitai are a corps of elite retainers who rose to defend the Shogunate in its final days. Trained in both traditional and modern warfare, they embody the spirit of the old samurai while adapting to the new age. Their resolve in battle is legendary.

The Shinsengumi are a corps of loyalists formed to protect the Shogunate's interests in Kyoto. Renowned for their strict discipline and unmatched swordsmanship, they strike fear into rebels and ronin alike. Their loyalty is absolute, and their blades swift.

Aizu Kotetsu is a feared street boss who serves as an unofficial enforcer for the Aizu clan in Kyoto. His crew handles the dirty work the samurai cannot, using local influence and hard violence to protect Aizu interests in the back alleys of the capital.

The people of Kanto, the spiritual homeland of the samurai class, live in a predominantly flat region that is perfect for extensive agriculture and the breeding of its renowned battle steeds, which yield abundant harvests and allow Kanto to field and maintain cavalry forces more easily. Imbued with the secular martial tradition in which they have their roots, the lords of Kanto can more easily raise large armies to face their enemies, but their great emphasis on military preparedness makes it more expensive to pay the wages of their soldiers.{newline}{newline}Foreign Merchant: Dutch

One of the most powerful tozama domains of the late Tokugawa period, the Satsuma Domain commands the southern tip of Kyushu with a proud samurai tradition and an eye toward modern reform. Governed by the Shimazu clan, Satsuma fields a disciplined military bolstered by imported Western firearms and artillery, alongside fiercely loyal retainers hardened by centuries of internal strife and external ambition. Though officially loyal to the shogunate, Satsuma grows increasingly defiant, backing the sonnō jōi movement while quietly forging alliances with other anti-Tokugawa domains. With its strong economy, built on barely legal trade through the Ryukyu Islands, and its modernizing army, the Satsuma-han is poised to play a decisive role in the struggle for Japan's future.

The First Choshu Expedition has ended with a whimper, rather than a roar. Under the leadership of Saigo Takamori, a light punishment has been enforced, and several retainers of Choshu have committed seppuku to apologize for the Kinmon Incident.
Choshu has forced back the Shogunate forces, showing the weakness of the Shogunate more clearly than ever before.

Choshu's assault on Kyoto has ended in defeat. Repelled at the Forbidden Gates, the domain is now condemned as a rebel force. With imperial approval secured, the Shogunate has called its allied domains to arms and begun a grand punitive campaign. If they crush Choshu's remaining resistance, the Bakufu's authority will be restored across Japan.

The Genji loyalists have been crushed, and the Shogunate’s authority stands unshaken. The reformist leaders have been executed or driven into hiding, while the conservative factions reassert their dominance in Choshu. Any hope of Choshu once again opposing the Shogunate is gone.
The Seigi-ha have risen up at Kosanji Temple, challenging the conservative faction in Choshu, who have been cracking down on the radicals ever since the domain's loss in the First Choshu Expedition.

Ah, you wish to understand our ranks. A student begins as an Keppan, to learn the basics of the art. Once they have achieved this, they will be granted a Mokuroku, a catalogue speaking of their relation to the school and the arts they have learned.

Once a student has learned most of our arts, they are granted the rank of Menkyo, and have the right to teach our techniques and represent our school in formal matches. Finally, there is the rank of Menkyo-Kaiden, signifying complete mastery of our arts. At this point, there is nothing left to learn.
Te-awase, or 'linking hands,' is simple sparring within the dojo. Through these, students may improve themselves without fear.

Tameshi-ai, the 'assessment match,' are matches between two students with wooden blades. These matches, inside or between dojos, are meant to improve oneself, not to harm, though their results may reflect upon the school. Only those who have received a Mokuroku may participate.

Taryu-shiai, 'inter-school matches,' are the true competitions. Fought between schools, usually without sharp weapons. Blows are often pulled, but serious injury can occur. A win can bring us great renown, while a loss will shame us deeply, so only Menkyo may fight in a Taryu-shiai.

Menko-Kaiden holders may attempt dojo-yaburi, 'dojo breaking.' One challenges the head of another school. Victory can abolish that dojo, while failure brings dishonor, loss of status, or exile. Such trials are rare, and often involve many students or careful strategy.

The most deadly of all duels are Shinken-Shobu, 'win-lose by real sword,' which are duels to the death. These are usually illegal, and the government only allows them under strict circumstances: a legal vendetta, the orders of a lord, or to right an honorable wrong. These reflect greatly upon our dojo, so none but those who have reached the rank of Menkyo-Kaiden may fight them.

Your father was a court noble, advising the emperor himself. While he held no actual power, none dared touch him, and even Daimyo would turn their ears to listen when he spoke. He made his living tutoring noble sons, and he taught you alongside them.

Your father was a humble but skilled swordsmith who through his physical strength and mastery of his art was able to transform raw metal into sharp blades, making him well known in his domain for the quality of his creations. Even as a child, by helping him in the forge, you were able to absorb some of his craftmanship and harden your body.

Your father was a prominent rice trader whose warehouses and counting houses stood at the heart of a bustling castle town. In an age when rice was the very measure of wealth, his keen eye for markets and relentless bargaining brought the family immense prosperity—indeed, far greater wealth than that possessed by most samurai. Though officially beneath the buke, your household enjoyed comforts that many samurai could only envy.

One of the 'One Hundred Surnames', your father was a farmer in a rural village. His farm was larger than most in the village, making him highly influential. Even so, he had to pay almost half of his harvest in the nengu tax to the daimyo each year.

Living on the outskirts of his village, your father was a skilled hunter, well-versed in tracking and chasing his prey through the woods and mountains. and taking it down with a swift stroke of his bow. Even if the rewards of his labour were barely enough for a humble life in the countryside, your father passed on much of his knowledge to you.

Your father was a kabuki actor whose dramatic performances drew large crowds in the pleasure districts of the great cities. Though adored by common townsfolk and celebrated for his striking stage presence, he was nevertheless dragged down by his status among the Eta-Hinin, the lowest social class in Japan. Fame and applause brought your family notoriety and a modest living, but admiration rarely translated into respect.

You spent your adolescence days training your sword skills together with other kids. Whether it was with real blades or improvised ones, in actual practice or imaginary duels, you improved your slashes and parries with no need to roll around.

You spent your adolescence working in a forge as the apprentice of a master swordsmith, learning the secrets of forge and blade in equal measure. By the end of your apprenticeship, you were able to forge a sword discreetly on your own, and why not, even swing it around.
